adjusted_or_95ci: Non-Hispanic White (vs Hispanic) 1.10 (0.52–2.30); Non-Hispanic Other/Multiple (vs Hispanic) 2.39 (0.49–11.57); Non-Hispanic Black (vs Hispanic) 2.81* (1.13–6.96); Non-Hispanic Asian (vs Hispanic) 3.48* (1.31–9.25)
literature: Black patients: more discontinuation, HR 1.43 (1.17–1.74) vs White (Ellis 2004); lower adherence, unadjusted OR 0.76 (Escobar 2025), RR 0.66 (Basios 2025). Hispanic patients: much lower adherence, unadjusted OR 0.21 vs White (Escobar 2025).
consistent: Partly. Yes for Black patients. The Hispanic gap is much smaller in our data. Our odds ratios use Hispanic as the reference group.

eda_discontinued_vs_continued: Good, fair, or poor mental health: 59.8% vs 41.6%
adjusted_or_95ci: Very good (vs Excellent) 1.67 (0.88–3.19); Fair (vs Excellent) 3.72* (1.45–9.53); Good (vs Excellent) 3.81* (1.98–7.34); Poor (vs Excellent) 9.50* (1.76–51.25)
literature: Depression: 1.76x the odds of nonadherence (95% CI 1.33–2.57), similar for hyperlipidemia/hypertension (Grenard 2011); lower statin adherence, RR 0.89 (Basios 2025). Antidepressant use not associated with discontinuation, OR 0.89 (0.75–1.06) (Halava 2016).
consistent: Mostly. Same direction as both meta-analyses; one cohort found no link. We measure self-rated mental health, not diagnosed or treated depression.

literature: Polypharmacy (5+ drugs): higher statin adherence, RR 1.32. The authors note this contrasts with earlier reports (Basios 2025).
consistent: Yes. More distinct drugs, lower odds of discontinuation.

driver: Only one statin fill in rounds 1-2
literature: 12% of Finnish statin initiators filled only one prescription in their first year; that study uses a single fill to define discontinuation (Halava 2016).
consistent: Not tested as a predictor in the literature. Not significant in the weighted model (significant only unweighted).

literature: Higher copay, faster discontinuation: HR 4.30 (3.39–5.44) for $20+ vs <$10 per month (Ellis 2004); OR 1.29 (1.03–1.62) for >20 vs <5 euros (Halava 2016).
consistent: No. Not significant in either inference model. Statins are now mostly low-cost generics, so costs in our cohort are low and vary little; 107 events also limit power.

literature: Medicare vs. private insurance: higher adherence, unadjusted OR 1.22 (Escobar 2025).
consistent: Same direction in unadjusted data. Not significant after adjustment; Medicare overlaps with age.

literature: More comorbidity, better persistence: vascular comorbidity OR 0.80 (Halava 2016); 2+ comorbidities RR 1.25 (Basios 2025); high Charlson index, unadjusted OR 1.43 for adherence (Escobar 2025).
consistent: Same direction, not significant after adjustment. Our count covers all active conditions, not cardiovascular ones specifically.

literature: Older age, less discontinuation: HR 0.99 per year (Ellis 2004); OR 0.82 for 61–75 vs 24–50 (Halava 2016); higher adherence in older adults, RR 1.34 (Basios 2025).
consistent: Same direction. Our adjusted estimate per year is close to Ellis 2004 but not significant.

literature: Not reported separately in the reviewed studies.
consistent: Not tested. Discontinued patients have fewer fills, but the adjusted OR is above 1 once distinct drugs are held constant. The two are correlated, so read them together.

literature: Women: slightly more discontinuation, HR 1.18 (Ellis 2004); lower adherence, RR 0.92 (Basios 2025). No difference in Halava 2016 (OR 1.01).
consistent: No association in our data. The published effect is small and mixed.

literature: Medicaid vs. private insurance: lower adherence, unadjusted OR 0.77 (Escobar 2025).
consistent: Same direction in unadjusted data. Not significant after adjustment.

literature: Uninsured patients are not reported separately in the reviewed studies.
consistent: Not tested. Our largest unadjusted gap, but only 47 uninsured patients, so the adjusted OR is not significant and SHAP ranks it low.
